prompt: We're adding single sign-on with external identity providers to Platform+, our B2B web app. The design is in docs/design/sso-sign-in.md. We had an account takeover incident last quarter (see context/incident-report-2024-08.md), and I'm worried we might be repeating mistakes or creating new risks. Our security policy has specific requirements for sessions and tokens. Look through the design and supporting context files, then write your review to REVIEW.md at the top of the project. In your review, explain what's wrong and what needs to change. End the review with a fenced json list of findings, each with location (the section number of the document, like 3.2), severity (critical, high, medium, low or nit), issue and fix. Focus on concrete problems that affect security, compliance, or reliability—not style or formatting.

rubric.criterion: Each important finding explains the concrete consequence in this project and proposes a fix a developer can act on, without inventing problems that don't exist (code cannot check this because it requires understanding technical context and judging relevance).

findingsKey.finding: The authorization flow omits the nonce parameter required by OpenID Connect to prevent replay attacks.
Accounts are linked by matching email addresses without verifying the email_verified claim, enabling account takeover if an IdP provides unverified emails.
Session tokens stored in browser localStorage violate the security policy that prohibits localStorage for tokens and requires HTTP-only cookies.
90-day session duration exceeds the 30-day maximum specified in the security policy, increasing exposure window from account takeover incidents.
Sessions persist without back-channel revocation checks despite the security policy requiring them when supported, allowing continued access after IdP revocation.
JWKS fetched once at deploy and cached indefinitely contradicts the configuration template requiring refresh every 24 hours minimum, risking signature validation failures after key rotation.
Wildcard redirect URI pattern allows any subdomain to receive authentication codes, enabling potential open redirect attacks if subdomains are compromised.

State parameter described as 32 bytes but RFC 6749 recommends a minimum of 128 bits (16 bytes) with 256 bits (32 bytes) being reasonable for high-security applications, though not strictly a violation.

items.text: Asks why PKCE is not mentioned for the SPA authorization code flow despite being a security best practice for public clients.
items.source: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700 (IETF Trust Legal Provisions)

items.text: Notes missing rate limiting on SSO callback endpoints which could enable denial of service attacks against token validation.
items.source: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.text: Identifies missing audit trail for account linking events which would be critical for security investigations after potential compromises.

items.text: Asks about the user experience for IdP selection when users have access to multiple configured identity providers.

items.text: Notes that storing client secrets in version-controlled YAML files contradicts the twelve-factor app principle of storing secrets in environment variables.
Questions how the system handles gradual degradation when external IdP latency exceeds service level targets without cascading failures.
Asks about the plan for detecting and responding to IdP metadata changes that could break authentication flows without manual intervention.

weakAnswers: The design seems comprehensive and addresses the main requirements adequately.
Consider adding more information about scalability as the user base grows.
Good document structure but could benefit from additional diagrams for clarity.
Make sure to implement all security best practices during development.
The approach looks reasonable but needs more detail on error handling scenarios.

verdicts.note: Prompt does not name review method, hint at planted problems, or give the number of issues.
Clear what to review (design doc + context), where to write (REVIEW.md), and output format (JSON with location, severity, issue, fix).

Most issues explicitly stated and easy to find, but k1 (nonce) requires OIDC expertise and k5 (back-channel revocation) requires cross-referencing security policy. Differentiation between shallow and deep review is reasonable.
All 8 key items are verifiable in the fixture at the specified sections. Fix words align with solution content. Grader can match by section number.
No comments, test names, or file names point at planted problems. Fixture contains legitimate context files.
